title: Hard to be called a Muslim
word: Hard to be called a Muslim
hook: it is hard to be called a true Muslim; first love the faith and let go of pride (Majh ki Var, ang 141)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a knife of an age: kings turned butcher, truth's moon hidden, and Nanak still searching the dark. Today the ballad turns from kings to the name a person carries.

A cast-iron pan comes out of the back of a cupboard, orange with rust. Steel wool, hot water, patience, and slowly the dark metal shows again. Nobody calls it clean until it is. Guru Nanak lived among Hindus and Muslims, and in his ballad in Majh he speaks to his Muslim neighbors in the words of their own faith. He doesn't tell anyone to stop being a Muslim. He says something harder, in plain English: it's difficult to be called a Muslim. Only if you truly are one should you be called one.
screen: `A RUSTY PAN, SCOURED.` → `NANAK SPEAKS TO HIS NEIGHBORS.` → `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM.`

segments.voice: The salok goes on, not word for word. First, let the faith be sweet to you. Scrape away pride in your wealth, the way rust is scraped from metal. Become a true follower of the faith, and be rid of doubt about death and life. Accept God's will as above your head. Trust the Creator, and lose your self-importance. Be kind to every living being, says Nanak, and then you may be called a Muslim. Notice how high the bar is, and whose bar it is. Its words, din, faith; raza, God's will; mihar, mercy, are words his Muslim neighbors used for their own faith. He isn't laying a new standard over them; he's taking their own words seriously and asking that they be lived all the way through. A few lines before, on ang one hundred forty, he does the same with the outward signs. In paraphrase: let mercy be your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and honest living your Quran. Modesty, good conduct, truth: each a practice of the faith, lived inside. And the salok mocks no one. Elsewhere on this path Nanak asks the same of pandits and yogis: live what your name promises. Muslims here are honored by being held to their own best words. Notice the order, too. First, sweetness, before rules or outward signs. The salok calls this hard. It doesn't call it impossible. That's today's line: hard to be true.
screen: `FIRST, LET THE FAITH BE SWEET.` · `SCRAPE AWAY PRIDE LIKE RUST.` · `MERCY BE YOUR MOSQUE.` · `BE KIND TO EVERY BEING.` · then, large: `HARD TO BE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Name quietly what you're called: the faith you belong to, the one you're learning, or a simpler name like friend, parent, neighbor. Ask gently what that name promises, find one word in it, kindness, honesty, patience, mercy, and hold it for a few breaths. If you pray, offer that word to God in the way your own tradition prays.
Hard to be called a Muslim. Guru Nanak's salok in Majh ki Var: let the faith be sweet, scrape away pride, accept God's will, be kind to every being, and then be called by the name. Today's word.
screen: `HARD TO BE CALLED A MUSLIM — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: hard to be true. Hard, and still worth the scouring, like that old pan. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: These saloks are sung and read as part of Majh ki Var in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in katha they are explained as Guru Nanak asking people of every faith to live what their own faith teaches.

original.note: musalman kahavan muskal: 'it is hard to be called a Muslim', the salok's opening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line criticizing another faith.
what it means: Guru Nanak holds Muslims to Islam's own best words, and the same bar runs through his words to every path.
what a scholar hears: some readers hear sound-play in the salok, musalman, muskal (hard), maskal (a polisher's tool for rust), so the name itself carries the work.
guess: a name earned by living the faith's own best words
a saying that faith is too hard for most people
a rule that only scholars may call themselves Muslim

chat.says: In that salok, did Guru Nanak tell Muslims to stop being Muslims?
options: No. He held them to their own faith's words: let it be sweet, drop pride, be kind to all.
Yes. He said it was too hard, so they should follow his way instead.
No. He said outward signs alone, like the mosque, are what make a Muslim.
chat.meaning: The salok honors Muslims by their own words, din, raza, mihar: let the faith be sweet, scrape away pride, be kind to every being.

din.meaning: faith; a word his Muslim neighbors used for their own

notes: Ang 141 salok paraphrased from ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵਣੁ ਮੁਸਕਲੁ ਜਾ ਹੋਇ ਤਾ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵੈ ॥ ਅਵਲਿ ਅਉਲਿ ਦੀਨੁ ਕਰਿ ਮਿਠਾ ਮਸਕਲ ਮਾਨਾ ਮਾਲੁ ਮੁਸਾਵੈ ... ਤਉ ਨਾਨਕ ਸਰਬ ਜੀਆ ਮਿਹਰੰਮਤਿ ਹੋਇ ਤ ਮੁਸਲਮਾਣੁ ਕਹਾਵੈ.
